1.pericope_label: Then I looked, and, behold, in the firmament that was above the head of the cherubims there appeared over them as it were a sapphire stone, as the appearance of the likeness of a throne. And he spake unto the man clothed with linen, and said, Go in between the wheels, even under the cherub, and fill thine hand with coals of fire from between the cherubims, and scatter them over the city. And he went in in my sight. Now the cherubims stood on the right side of the house, when the man went in; and the cloud filled the inner court. Then the glory of the Lord went up from the cherub, and stood over the threshold of the house; and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was full of the brightness of the Lord’s glory.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter exactly, the first eight verses showing how the city is to be burned and the rest how Jehovah will forsake his temple; Ellicott notes that no being is named on the throne though the next verse implies one, that the man clothed in linen who had been employed in mercy is now made the agent of judgment, and that the singular cherub for the usual plural is obscure, and marks the contrast with the dedication, when the same cloud filled the house as God came.

Gill calls it another vision, like the first in some things and different in others, serving partly for the burning of the city and partly for the Lord's removal, takes the man in linen for a figure of the invading army, and reads the cherubim's station on the right as the south side, farthest from the northern idolatries; Calvin states the design before the words, that God meant to bear witness that he had nothing further in common with them, forbids speculation about the right hand, and says the temple was stripped of its furniture, since without God what remained.

Clarke reads the removal as gradual, the divine presence withdrawing farther and farther from the temple, dates the coals to the burning by the Chaldeans, and stands back from the whole apparatus to call the vision a set of hieroglyphics by which the glory was in some measure represented.

Henry takes the throne devotionally and warns about the medium, since here is the invisible world set out in the visible, faint representations no more to be compared with the truth than a picture with the life, and marks that God is above the cherubim in dominion and not in dignity only.

debates.question: Who is the man clothed in linen?

positions.position: No angel at all, but a figure of the invading army.
The same person as before, whose change of office is the point: employed in mercy, he now executes judgment.

debates.question: When is the burning that the coals signify?

positions.position: The burning by the Chaldeans.
The Chaldean or the Roman army, the vision referring chiefly if not altogether to the later destruction.
A question of source rather than date: taken from between the cherubim, the coals signify that the doom is from God and not from man's will or any accident.

debates.question: May the detail of the vision be interpreted?

positions.position: Yes: the station on the right is the south side, farthest from the northern idolatries, so that they bear testimony against them.
No: we are not to seek cunning speculations about the right hand, the detail serving only to show the way open and the vision certain.
The whole is a set of hieroglyphics by which the glory was in some measure represented.

outliers.claim: Divides the chapter on its two errands, the first eight verses showing how the city is to be burned with fire and the remainder how Jehovah will forsake his temple.
Marks the contrast with the dedication of the temple, when the same cloud filled the house as God came, where here it fills the house as he departs.

5.pericope_label: And the sound of the cherubims’ wings was heard even to the outer court, as the voice of the Almighty God when he speaketh. And it came to pass, that when he had commanded the man clothed with linen, saying, Take fire from between the wheels, from between the cherubims; then he went in, and stood beside the wheels. And one cherub stretched forth his hand from between the cherubims unto the fire that was between the cherubims, and took thereof, and put it into the hands of him that was clothed with linen: who took it, and went out. And there appeared in the cherubims the form of a man’s hand under their wings.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the sound proof that the cherubim were already in motion, since when they stood they let their wings down, and works out the order of the narrative, denying that it is chronological: the verses about the coals are a parenthetical fuller account of what was mentioned briefly before, and the long description that follows is the first vision supplied in pieces as the narrative advances.

Gill hears the Gospel in the sound of the wings, a joyful noise of grace and pardon carried into all the earth by the swift ministry of the apostles; Calvin hears thunder, and makes the errand a demolition of confidence, since the Jews thought the sacred fire on the altar availed to expiate all wickedness while God so resided in the temple as to clothe himself with wrath, the cherubim keeping the very arms by which they were to be destroyed.

Clarke takes the sound for thunder, which was called the voice of God, and reconstructs the hand under the wings, holding that arms and wings were not distinct but that the arms were feathered and the long front feathers reached beyond the fingers.

Henry looks past the machinery to the omen it introduces, the departure of the glory that would open the door for ruin, so that those who had provoked God to go might know what they had lost and lament after him.

debates.question: What is the sound of the cherubim's wings?

positions.position: Evidence of motion: they had let their wings down when they stood, and were now on the eve of departure.
Thunder, which was called the voice of God.
The sound of the Gospel, carried into all the earth by the swift ministry of the apostles.

debates.question: What do the wings and the hand signify?

positions.position: Subordination: angels have no independent motion but are governed by a secret instinct, which is why they are winged in the sanctuary too.
Anatomy first, and then a moral: the arms were feathered like wings, and a human hand may signify that God helps and punishes man by man.
Simply the action, one of the four putting out his hand from among the rest.

outliers.claim: Denies that the chapter is chronological: the verses about the coals are not later in time but a parenthetical fuller account of what was mentioned briefly before, and the long description that follows is the first vision supplied in pieces as the narrative advances.
Makes the errand a demolition of confidence: the false and perverse glorying that had intoxicated them, that God was in some way bound to them exclusively, is cut away from under them.

9.pericope_label: And when I looked, behold the four wheels by the cherubims, one wheel by one cherub, and another wheel by another cherub: and the appearance of the wheels was as the colour of a beryl stone. And as for their appearances, they four had one likeness, as if a wheel had been in the midst of a wheel. When they went, they went upon their four sides; they turned not as they went, but to the place whither the head looked they followed it; they turned not as they went. And their whole body, and their backs, and their hands, and their wings, and the wheels, were full of eyes round about, even the wheels that they four had. As for the wheels, it was cried unto them in my hearing, O wheel. And every one had four faces: the first face was the face of a cherub, and the second face was the face of a man, and the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle. And the cherubims were lifted up. This is the living creature that I saw by the river of Chebar. And when the cherubims went, the wheels went by them: and when the cherubims lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the same wheels also turned not from beside them. When they stood, these stood; and when they were lifted up, these lifted up themselves also: for the spirit of the living creature was in them.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering that makes the cry a name given to the wheels, since it leaves the words in my hearing an unmeaning addition, and take the verb as addressing: the wheels were called on to whirl, and to verify their name.

Gill reads the whole machinery ecclesiologically, the wheels for churches and the cherubim for their ministers, the four sides for the uniformity of Gospel churches and the likeness of body and wings for the agreement of ministers in doctrine and work; Calvin reads the same parts providentially, wheels being the fittest image of change, drawn for us in concession to our weakness because profane men fabricate a blind fortune, and full of eyes because events hang on secret commands.

Clarke refuses the usual mechanics of a wheel within a wheel and conjectures two rims on a single axis, sorts out the versions of the stone, calls the received rendering of the cry the most unfortunate translation ever made, and infers from the change of face that a cherub was in the likeness of an ox; Wesley gives the stone as sea-green and puts the whole reading in a sentence, that events are determined not by the wheel of fortune, which is blind, but by the wheels of providence, which are full of eyes.

positions.position: The churches, with the cherubim for their ministers.
All the changes of the world, drawn under this figure because men otherwise fabricate a blind fortune.

debates.question: How is a wheel within a wheel to be understood?

positions.position: Not as one wheel cutting another at right angles, which would not account for the motions; rather a wheel with two rims on a single axis.
As one form common to all four, the appearance being the same though the variety darkens our eyes.

debates.question: What was cried to the wheels?

positions.position: Not a name at all: the received rendering is the most unfortunate ever made, the word meaning the roller, a chariot, or roll on.
Not a name but an address: the wheels were called on to whirl and verify their name.
A vocal direction, one guiding them.
God's voice, heard by every creature, so that no motion happens apart from that instinct.

outliers.claim: Turns on a preacher who took the exclamation to the wheels for a text and extracted the decree of eternal predestination from it, saying such working of God's word cannot be too severely reprehended.
Puts the providential reading in one sentence: events are not determined by the wheel of fortune, which is blind, but by the wheels of providence, which are full of eyes.

18.pericope_label: Then the glory of the Lord departed from off the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubims. And the cherubims lifted up their wings, and mounted up from the earth in my sight: when they went out, the wheels also were beside them, and every one stood at the door of the east gate of the Lord’s house; and the glory of the God of Israel was over them above. This is the living creature that I saw under the God of Israel by the river of Chebar; and I knew that they were the cherubims. Every one had four faces apiece, and every one four wings; and the likeness of the hands of a man was under their wings. And the likeness of their faces was the same faces which I saw by the river of Chebar, their appearances and themselves: they went every one straight forward.

schools.summary: Ellicott alone traces the departure as a sequence of stations, from the right side of the house to the threshold, then above the waiting cherubim, then up from the earth to the east gate, which is the main entrance of the outermost court; and he would strike the words every one as absent from the original, since they stood, or it stood, is better and the vision is to be taken as a whole.

Gill counts the move another step towards a general departure and another warning given, and takes the repeated identification as carrying an addition, that the figure on the throne is the God of Israel and therefore, since the Father never appeared in human form, that Christ is meant; Calvin puts the principal point plainly, that God had deserted the temple, and explains why they thought it impossible and why the vision had to be shown twice.

Clarke objects that the English plural ending should be uniformly expunged, and then admits he has met with nothing on the subject that entirely satisfies him, having tried only to make the literal meaning plain, since he does not like conjectures on divine things; Wesley names the east gate the court of the people, hears in the pause a respite of execution, and allows two ways the prophet may have known the creatures.

debates.question: What is to be made of the standing still?

positions.position: The words every one are not in the original and should be struck out; they stood, or it stood, is better, the vision being one whole.
The glory, the cherubim and the wheels all stood, respiting execution and giving opportunity of preventing the approaching misery.

debates.question: Why is the vision shown a second time?

positions.position: To carry an addition, that the figure on the throne is the God of Israel, and so to prove the deity of Christ.
As a confirmation, not for the prophet's private advantage but for the people, or at least to leave without excuse those who despised so manifest a favour.
The question is rather how the prophet knew them, and the answer is either special assurance or comparison with what he had often seen in the temple.

outliers.claim: Admits at the close that he has met with nothing on the subject that entirely satisfies him, and says why he stops at the literal meaning: he does not like conjectures on divine things, since many points which had no other origin are now incorporated with creeds that it is deemed sinful to doubt.

Explains the repetitions within the chapter by the temper of the hearers, a people dull and slow who added to their other faults an open endeavour to detract from the authority of every prophet, so that what was clear enough had to be inculcated again.
